title: Relational operators and floating point comparisons
recap: Relational operators compare operands and produce bool values. Direct equality is appropriate for many exact values, but rounding error makes == and != unreliable for calculated floating-point values.

A robust approximate comparison can combine an absolute tolerance near zero with a relative tolerance that scales to the larger magnitude. The comparison should use the absolute difference and accept it when it is no larger than the greater tolerance.
objectives: Observe why direct equality can reject a calculated floating-point value.
Implement a combined relative and absolute approximate comparison.
Use std::abs and std::max to compare magnitudes.
Reject values outside the selected tolerance.
warnings: A single fixed epsilon is not suitable across every magnitude.
Do not compare only one signed subtraction; use the absolute difference.
Tolerance values should reflect the precision required by the problem domain.
challenge: Implement approximatelyEqualRelAbs(). It should compare the absolute difference with the greater of an absolute epsilon and a relative epsilon scaled by the larger operand magnitude. Demonstrate that 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly equal to 0.3, is approximately equal, and is not approximately equal to 0.31.
hints: Compute the larger magnitude with std::max(std::abs(a), std::abs(b)).

contains: bool approximatelyEqualRelAbs(double a, double b, double relEpsilon, double absEpsilon)
